outcome: Xinyao Zhang posted a preprint (Nov 2024, revised through Jul 2025) claiming to remove the last obstruction (the p=3 exceptional case) in the two-dimensional regular Fontaine-Mazur conjecture over Q, which combined with Lue Pan's 2019/2021 work (covering p>=5) would complete the regular-case conjecture for all odd primes; separately, Jack Thorne posted a preprint (Aug 2026) proving further partial cases of the Fontaine-Mazur conjecture for GL(2), including some previously-open reducible-residual cases. Neither has been digested by an expert referee or accepted at a journal as of the search date.

disputes.summary: A third-party automated preprint-review site (Pith, which describes itself as producing machine-generated, referee-style reports) assessed Zhang's paper as 'clos[ing] Pan's p=3 gap with a promising strategy, but the written proof is too sketchy at the local epsilon=+-1 case to accept as is.' This is not a human expert's verdict, but no human expert digestion (journal referee report, seminar writeup, blog post) was found either, so the paper's correctness is unconfirmed by any authoritative source as of this search.

summary: The triage correctly identified the two relevant preprints. Zhang's paper (arXiv:2412.06812, v1 2024-11-30, latest v4 2025-07-22) explicitly presents itself as a sequel to Lue Pan's arXiv:1901.07166 (which had already established the regular-case Fontaine-Mazur conjecture for p>=5) and claims to remove the last remaining obstruction, the p=3 exceptional case, thereby claiming the regular-case conjecture for all odd primes. I checked the arXiv admin note flagging 'substantial text overlap with arXiv:1901.07166, arXiv:1005.2008 by other authors' and confirmed via the paper's own introduction that this reflects Zhang building explicitly and extensively on Pan's and Kisin's established results and setup (a normal sequel relationship, citing what it extends), not an impropriety; the paper's stated new contributions are a potential-pro-modularity argument working uniformly for all odd primes and a generalized Greenberg-Wiles formula for the p=3 case. No journal acceptance, MathOverflow discussion, Tao-blog coverage, or other human expert digestion of this specific paper was found in searches; the only third-party assessment located is an automated review site (Pith) that itself is AI/machine-generated rather than a human referee, and it flags a possible gap in the local epsilon=+-1 case. Given the absence of human expert verification, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved', with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the result, if correct, confirms the conjecture in this case; there is no counterexample). Jack Thorne's separate preprint (arXiv:2608.07186, 2026-08-07) proves additional GL(2) cases (potentially crystalline ordinary, Hodge-Tate weights {0,1}, totally odd determinant, including some previously-open reducible-residual cases at p=2), explicitly a partial-progress paper per its own framing ('the vast majority of cases... are known'), so it is recorded as informing the same 'claimed' picture but does not itself change the status classification (it is genuinely a case/partial result, consistent with partial-type progress, but since the overall conjecture status here already rests on the not-yet-digested Zhang claim, I keep a single status field per the harness's instruction to describe the decisive event and discuss the rest here). Neither paper's acknowledgements, introduction, or any secondary source mentions any AI system, language model, or AI-assisted tool contributing to the mathematics; Zhang thanks his supervisor Takeshi Saito and Kojiro Matsumoto, Thorne credits only ERC grant funding. A separate ScienceDaily story about 'Claude Fable 5' and a mathematician named Alpöge (checked because it surfaced in search results) concerns an unrelated problem, the Jacobian conjecture (a counterexample in dimension >=3), and does not mention Fontaine-Mazur at all — I confirmed this by fetching the article directly and am ruling it out explicitly rather than silently.
competing_reading: One could argue Zhang's result should be classified as 'resolved' if one takes the mathematical content of a careful, sequel-style preprint from a specialist working under a named advisor at face value, especially since no substantive rebuttal or identified error (beyond the automated reviewer's flag) has surfaced in nearly two years since posting. Conversely, one could argue for 'open' if the automated reviewer's flagged gap at the local epsilon=+-1 case is treated as a live, unresolved correctness concern rather than routine preprint uncertainty. I chose 'claimed' as the middle reading most consistent with §6.1's literal test (no expert digestion, no journal acceptance) while acknowledging the claim is fairly mature (multiple self-revisions over 8 months, no public rebuttal).
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance, a human referee report, a seminar or conference talk with expert Q&A, a MathOverflow/blog discussion by a specialist in Galois deformation theory, or a follow-up paper by another author citing Zhang's p=3 result as an established input, would move this from 'claimed' to 'resolved'. Conversely, a substantive erratum, withdrawal, or identified error in the local epsilon=+-1 case would move it toward 'progress'/'incident'.
